## Geometry Design Principles

### Forest-Hirata bundles versus differential geometry

The Forest-Hirata appendix gives a clean abstract reformulation of local
element placement [@foresthirata]. The lattice is treated as a fibre bundle
over the machine loop; local neighbourhoods are element intervals; the fibres
may be coordinate frames, particle coordinates, maps, or envelopes; and the
matching block between local descriptions is a transition function
$g_{ij}\in G$.

The present OPALX note uses a more concrete differential-geometric language.
Each element may carry a reference path $\Gamma_i(\ell)$, a moving orthonormal
frame, marked interface charts, and a placed support region in laboratory
space. This is closer to implementation because it directly supports field
evaluation, aperture checks, and coordinate conversion inside an element.

The two viewpoints answer different questions:

1. use differential geometry locally inside an element whenever a curved or
   adapted chart is numerically useful;
2. use fibre-bundle-style transition maps to connect neighboring charts,
   branches, anchors, and closures without pretending that there must be one
   globally preferred frame.

### Current OPALX implementation context

The current tracker advances particles in physical time. Ordinary particle
transport uses a Boris-Buneman update. Elements have rigid spatial placement
and local field frames; field assembly uses orbit-threader support queries
or specialized spatial selection for compatible analytic rings.

The port graph, generalized placement tuple and dynamic-motion transforms
below are proposed extensions. They do not describe an existing general
port-graph implementation.

### A geometry graph and placement tuple

The cleanest generalization is to represent machine geometry by a directed
placement graph

$$
\mathcal G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E) .
$$

In this proposed graph, $\mathcal N$ contains named ports, free anchors and,
when needed, internal junction nodes. Each edge in $\mathcal E$ represents
a two-ended connection or a two-port placed object. A multiport object, such
as a splitter, requires an explicit internal subgraph rather than one ordinary
directed edge. Physics elements, drifts and geometry-only operators can be
represented within this convention.

This representation unifies linear and circular machines immediately:

1. a transfer line is an open connected path in $\mathcal G$ with two exposed
   boundary ports,
2. a ring is a closed cycle in $\mathcal G$,
3. a sector machine is a subgraph together with one or more symmetry
   transforms that replicate it.

Every two-port placed object $i$ should be representable by a tuple

$$
\mathfrak E_i=
\bigl(
M_i,\,
U_i,\,
\Omega_i,\,
\psi_i,\,
p_i^{\mathrm{in}},\,
p_i^{\mathrm{out}},\,
A_i,\,
B_i,\,
\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{err}},\,
\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{dyn}}(t),\,
\tau_i
\bigr) .
$$

Here $M_i$ is the physics model, $U_i$ the canonical local chart,
$\Omega_i\subset U_i$ the local support, $\psi_i$ the intrinsic geometry map,
and $p_i^{\mathrm{in}}$ and $p_i^{\mathrm{out}}$ the named ports. For the
displayed active-pose products, define $A_i$ to map canonical element
coordinates into entrance-port coordinates, and $B_i$ to map exit-port
coordinates into canonical element coordinates. Products act right to left.
The static correction $\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{err}}$ and dynamic correction
$\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{dyn}}(t)$ are expressed in that canonical frame;
$\tau_i$ denotes timing metadata. These are conventions of the proposed model,
not the direction of the current stored `CoordinateSystemTrafo` objects.

If $T(p_i^{\mathrm{in}})$ denotes the laboratory-frame pose of the entrance
port, then the runtime pose of the canonical element frame is

$$
T_i(t)=T(p_i^{\mathrm{in}})\,A_i\,\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{err}}\,\Delta T_i^{\mathrm{dyn}}(t) .
$$

The corresponding exit-port pose is

$$
T(p_i^{\mathrm{out}},t)=T_i(t)\,B_i .
$$

### Transition maps as first-class objects

Whenever two local charts meet, OPALX should store two closely related pieces
of information:

1. the rigid port-to-port patch transform $C_{pq}$ attached to the named
   interface;
2. the induced change from chart $j$ to chart $i$,
   $g_{ij}(u_j,t)=P_i^{-1}(P_j(u_j,t),t)$, restricted to points for which
   $P_j(u_j,t)\in P_i(U_i,t)$ and the local inverse exists.

For compatible Cartesian port frames, the frame change can be represented
by the rigid patch transform $C_{pq}$. A coordinate change between curved
element charts also includes their intrinsic maps and need not be rigid:

$$g_{ij}=\psi_i^{-1}\circ T_i^{-1}\circ T_j\circ\psi_j,$$

on the domain where these local maps and inverses exist. Sharing only a face
does not by itself make the chart-coordinate map rigid.

### Two complementary coordinate charts

For OPALX it is useful to distinguish explicitly between:

1. a **reference chart** $s$ for lattice description, sequence order,
   optics-style diagnostics, and survey reports;
2. a **world chart** $(\mathbf r,t)$ for actual field evaluation, particle
   pushing, aperture collisions, and self-field coupling.

In a purely MAD-X-like mode the two charts nearly collapse onto one another. In
a time-based OPALX mode they do not. The code should therefore allow both to
coexist without forcing one to masquerade as the other.

### Minimal front-end semantics

The front-end syntax should compile to the graph-based placement model above.
The intent is to extend the present manual concepts rather than replace them
with an unrelated syntax.

| Input notion | Current status | Proposed semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `LINE` | Implemented ordered sequence | Represent as an ordered open path in the proposed placement graph. |
| `RING` | Implemented periodic sequence topology | Represent as a cycle; geometric closure and closed-orbit conditions remain separate. |
| Line origin and explicit element poses | Implemented | Reuse these poses as roots or anchors; generic named free anchors would be an extension. |
| `ELEMEDGE` | Implemented reference-coordinate placement | Compile into element transforms; keep reference-coordinate bookkeeping distinct from field-support selection. |
| Alignment errors | Implemented static misalignment transform | Relate the stored parent-to-local transform to the proposed active correction explicitly. |
| Named ports and patch objects | Proposed extension | Declare interface charts, geometry transforms and closure constraints independently of physics elements. |
| Generic chart, support and timing attributes | Proposed extension | Define any `STRAIGHT`, `ARC` or `USER` syntax and dynamic timing semantics before exposing them as an input interface. |
